response.text:
Because the whale-fleet knows a class of officers unknown elsewhere—the harpooneers—here fits a domestic peculiarity. In the old Dutch Fishery, command was divided between the captain and an officer called the Specksnyder—literally, Fat-Cutter; usage made it Chief Harpooneer. Navigation and general management were the captain’s; all whale-hunting concerns the Specksnyder’s. In the British Greenland Fishery, under the corrupted title Specksioneer, he lingers, abridged; now but senior harpooneer, one of the captain’s subalterns. Yet upon the harpooneers’ good conduct the voyage largely depends; and in the American Fishery, under certain circumstances (night watches on a whaling ground) the command of the ship’s deck may be his. Therefore the sea’s grand maxim demands he live nominally apart from the men forward and be marked their professional superior—though familiarly their social equal.

At sea the grand distinction is this: officer aft, man forward. Hence mates quarter with the captain; and, in most American whalers, the harpooneers too take their meals in the captain’s cabin and sleep near it.

Though a Southern whaling voyage (by far the longest made by man), with its perils and community of interest, may in some cases beget a less rigorous discipline; yet, never mind how much like an old Mesopotamian family these whalemen may, in some primitive instances, live together; for all that, the punctilious externals, at least, of the quarter-deck are seldom materially relaxed, and in no instance done away. Many a Nantucket skipper parades with an elated grandeur not surpassed in any military navy; nay, extorting almost as much outward homage as if he wore the imperial purple, and not the shabbiest of pilot-cloth. And though of all men the moody captain of the Pequod was the least given to that shallowest assumption; though the only homage he ever exacted was implicit, instantaneous obedience; though he required no man to remove the shoes from his feet ere stepping upon the quarter-deck; and though there were times, owing to peculiar circumstances hereafter to be detailed, when he addressed them in unusual terms, whether of condescension or in terrorem; yet even Ahab was by no means unobservant of the paramount forms and usages of the sea.

Nor will it fail to be perceived that behind those forms he sometimes masked himself; making use of them for private ends. That certain sultanism of his brain, else in good degree unmanifested, through those forms became incarnate in irresistible dictatorship. For be a man’s intellectual superiority what it will, it can never assume the practical, available supremacy over other men without the aid of some sort of external arts and entrenchments—always, in themselves, more or less paltry and base. This it is, that for ever keeps God’s true princes of the Empire from the world’s hustings; and leaves the highest honors that this air can give, to those men who become famous more through their infinite inferiority to the choice hidden handful of the Divine Inert, than through their undoubted superiority over the dead level of the mass. Such large virtue lurks in these small things when extreme political superstitions invest them, that in some royal instances even to idiot imbecility they have imparted potency. But when, as with Nicholas the Czar, the ringed crown encircles an imperial brain, the plebeian herds crouch abased before the tremendous centralization. Let the tragic dramatist who would depict indomitableness remember the hint.

But Ahab, my Captain, still moves before me in all his Nantucket grimness and shagginess; and in this episode touching Emperors and Kings, I must not conceal that I have only to do with a poor old whale-hunter like him; and, therefore, all outward majestical trappings and housings are denied me. Oh, Ahab! what shall be grand in thee, it must needs be plucked at from the skies, and dived for in the deep, and featured in the unbodied air!
